responseSet.title: Margaret Lowenfeld: An Appreciation of Her Contribution to Child Psychology
responseSet.authorMast: Phyllis M. Traill and  John Hood-Williams
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Margaret Lowenfeld: An Appreciation of Her Contribution to Child Psychology

Phyllis Traill MA DIPICP and John Hood-Williams MA DIPICP

John Hood-Williams

John Hood-Williams  

Dr. Margaret Lowenfeld died on February 2nd, 1973, aged almost 83. She had continued to work until a few months before her death.

When she started in private paediatric practice in 1928 she was able to develop the interest in the psychological aspects of children's diseases which had been stimulated by her earlier medical research work on acute rheumatism linked to social conditions and on the study of some aspects of lactation. It was then that she started the Children's Centre in Clarendon Road, W.11, a voluntary body for children whose parents could not afford private fees.

The Children's Centre grew, in 1932, into the Institute of Child Psychology with its own premises. A Child Guidance team operated here, to which were added, as honorary consultants, a paediatrician, a gynaecologist and a parents’ physician. From the outset an approach was established which took into account the whole child and his parents. A reason for including a gynaecologist in the team was that in those days many mothers’ emotional difficulties were sometimes caused by, sometimes enhanced by, minor gynaecological conditions, so draggingly enervating that they could affect the whole family's well-being and which could easily be rectified; but at that time they were not attended to in the routine way they are nowadays. The parents’ physician would undertake psychotherapy with a few disturbed parents.

A department for physical re-education was also established where a skilled practitioner, using the technique of allowing the child to play with physical apparatus, would help him to “make friends” with his own body and gain pleasure and efficiency from using it better.

In 1933, she started the three-year course to train Child Psychotherapists which has continued to the present day and this course is still teaching the approach to Child Psychotherapy that she originated.

When she started the Children's Centre (in 1928), knowledge of the emotional development of children was based almost entirely on findings from the psychoanalysis of adult patients and the retrospective reconstructions of their childhood. She realised that play is the natural mode of expression for a child, so set about studying what children actually do when allowed to play freely in the presence of friendly and unobtrusive adults who do not impose the adult point of view. They could also be used as play material themselves or as helpers to assist the child to realise his play intention. The original range of play material was added to as the children asked for it; it was they who indicated their needs. Never before had such a study been undertaken.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A Day Centre for Disturbed Young Children and Their Parents**

Arnon Bentovim and Mary Boston

Mary Boston

Great Ormond Street, London

Mary Boston  

Introduction

Although there is an extensive network of educational facilities for the disturbed school-age child, it has been increasingly felt that there is a role for the Day Centre or Hospital where psychiatric care can be given to patients for several hours daily. Units for children vary in aims and methods but all attempt to meet a need met neither by ordinary out-patient or child guidance clinics nor by the very limited in-patient facilities available, nor by special school facilities.

Connell (1961) in his description of a day hospital for children stressed the importance of the continuous availability of psychiatric staff and medical resources and a flexible approach to the child's and the family's needs.

In the area of the pre-school child, although there are strident demands for nursery schools or play-groups to help to meet early educational and social needs, facilities to deal with disturbance in the young child and his family are few. Frommer (1967) has suggested that a special day centre for the treatment of a variety of psychiatric and chronic medical problems in pre-school children may not only be more economical but even preferable to individual treatment.

Other centres such as the Child Development Centre in New York (Landauer 1966) combine attendance at a therapeutic nursery, with individual or group therapy for parents. Anna Freud (1966) has described the interaction of the Hampstead Child Therapy Course and Clinic with the pre-nursery groups, and nursery schools for blind and sighted children. Teuens (1966) described a therapeutic day nursery providing group work for a variety of children and finding that quite severely disturbed children may be helped.

Great Ormond Street Day Centre

Although children of all ages are seen in the Department of Psychological Medicine of The Hospital for Sick Children, our close relationship to the paediatric side of the Hospital, both in-patient and out-patient, results in our seeing a larger proportion of children under five years of age, (25-30% of the total as compared to one in ten in many child guidance clinics).

[[RunningHead]]

Training at the Society of Analytical Psychology

Dorothy Davidson

Dorothy Davidson

Dorothy Davidson  

The Society of Analytical Psychology (London) was founded in 1944. Its first President was Professor C. G. Jung who was the originator of the form of Psycho-analysis adapted and named by him Analytical Psychology. The Society has established professional standards and is the recognised qualifying body for Jungian Analysts (Analytical Psychologists) in Great Britain. Its headquarters are at 30 Devonshire Place, London, W.1.

Over the years of training candidates to qualify as Analytical Psychologists to work with adults; through writing and discussions of the basic theoretical and clinical concepts of Jung's work; and through the experience of clinical practice, ideas have been germinating and growing within the Society towards the setting up of an additional training for people wishing to work with children. These ideas have now taken root and a training has been established.

It will enable successful candidates, both medical and lay, to practise as Child Analytic Psychologists. It will also qualify them to apply for membership of the Association of Child Psychotherapists, thus equipping them to work in the Education and Health Services as Child Psychotherapists.

The minimum length of training is three years but all candidates are required to have 400 hours personal analysis with a training analyst of the Society prior to being formally accepted for the three year training.

Medical candidates should have had some experience of working with children, e.g., Paediatrics, Child Guidance, Maternity and Child Welfare Clinics. Lay candidates should have an Honours degree in Psychology or equivalent subjects and some professional experience with children, e.g., Teaching, Child Care, Speech Therapy, Psychiatric Social Work and work in Children's Homes or Nurseries.

During the training, seminars will be held twice weekly at 30 Devonshire Place from 8.30 p.m. to 10.00 p.m. Each year will be divided into three terms. In the first year of training the trainee will share seminars with trainees engaged in the adult training and in the second term of that year the trainee will take on one adult patient for analysis under the supervision of one of the Society's approved analysts and will continue with that patient for at least two years.

responseSet.title: Short-Term Therapeutic Work with a Ten-Year-Old Girl
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Short-Term Therapeutic Work with a Ten-Year-Old Girl

Patricia Polke

Patricia Polke

Patricia Polke  

I saw Frances for five sessions, on a once weekly basis, when she was ten years old. I would like to focus on what occurred in those sessions, and to try to define some of the themes that appeared and the processes that I think occurred, in the light of it having been established that there would be a small number of interviews.

Frances’ parents had been attending the clinic regularly for over two years, in conjunction with the once weekly treatment of their elder daughter, Claire. (Frances also has a younger sister and brother.) Until this time the parents had not given their social worker any reason to believe that Frances’ development was causing any concern. Then, her mother mentioned that she had noticed that recently Frances was not sleeping, that she would hide under the bedclothes, that she needed the light on at night, and she was talking about a fear of ghosts. When the social worker suggested that Frances could come to someone at the clinic to talk about this her parents readily accepted this. I think that, for these parents, this ready acceptance was indicative of their trust in the social worker, in the clinic, and their belief that it is helpful to talk about things.

They stipulated that they only wanted Frances to come for a short period. Perhaps this was partly because it may have been too much to consider having two children in need of long-term help. Also, until this time it was probable that Frances had not indicated a need for help; in fact, as I hope to illustrate, it was probably clear to the parents that the occurrence of this fear of ghosts was something new in a child whose development was otherwise going well.

When I agreed to see Frances I did not know if her coming would be of any help, and, furthermore, if it was to be of any help, I did not know if seeing her for a few times would be sufficient. Two factors did seem to suggest that what I was offering might be helpful. One was that Frances herself had drawn her parents’ attention to her recent difficulties I think knowing they would probably try to get some help for her; and, secondly, Frances came from a family in which communication is good. This suggested that, if Frances did find her interviews helpful, this process could be further carried on in the family.

responseSet.title: Frances Tustin: Autism and Childhood Psychosis. The Hogarth Press, London, 1972. Price £2.50.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Frances Tustin: Autism and Childhood Psychosis. The Hogarth Press, London, 1972. Price £2.50.

Friedl Brown

Friedl Brown

Friedl Brown  

This is the kind of book we have long been in need of: nothing less than a “natural history” of the autistic child, and his development in therapy.

The book does many different things for us: it gives features to a notoriously blank landscape, focal points around which our observations can cluster and our intuitions gravitate. It throws light on the pre-conditions of developing the ability to think and to use symbols, in healthy children also. Furthermore, it throws light on the vestiges of autistic ways of functioning in ourselves, which can be such a help to our patients if we are in touch with them, or such a hindrance if we are not.

And most important it opens up a way of seeing things, and so gives existence to relations and feelings which previously, even when sensed, had to be put to one side, for there seemed to be no concepts, no vehicles on which they could ride into the light.

Mrs. Tustin describes pathological autism in terms of an attempt to establish an experience of continuity, of fusion with a containing mother, that either had been too harshly or too soon disrupted, or had only partially existed in the first place.

The state of being contained, of not yet being separated out, is part of the earliest condition of everyone; Mrs. Tustin calls it “normal primary autism”. To emerge from this stage and to become sufficiently contained in oneself to be a separate person with a “skin” round him (for example page 60), requires for the child to have had the experience of being “held” by a mother sensitive to him, in whose response he can find resonance of his own communications, who could in some way be experienced as giving him back to himself. The alternative to coming together in this way, is to have unbridgeable gaps in himself, “holes”, with their accompaniment of panic, irritation, helplessness, despair.

Mrs. Tustin's description of her autistic patients, as well as her quotations of other people's observations, brings the experience of the autistic child's situation vividly alive to us. In the second part of the book she gives a finely differentiated classification of the various kinds of autistic children (which are set out neatly in tabulated form) differentiating, among others, childhood schizophrenia, various kinds of pathological childhood autism, and “normal primary autism”.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Approach of Brief Conjoint Psychotherapy—A Case of Separation Anxiety

Ann Zadik

Ann Zadik

Ann Zadik  

In this paper I would like to describe the treatment of a mother and daughter, together.

As a child psychotherapist, newly trained, working very part-time in the busy, general medicine out-patient clinic of a suburban London hospital, I found myself face to face with the predicament of limited time and resources, combined with medical referrals of patients for specific problems.

I found the demands of this setting conducive to brief work.

As a learning experience, I wanted to attempt to bring psychotherapeutic skills, learned in intensive individual psychotherapy, to bear on the model of conjoint and brief work, undertaken together with a social worker. I undertook to keep clear, in my own mind, that although the approach was different, the basic assumptions inherent in the psychoanalytic process were the same. That is, I saw as central to our work to offer a safe setting in which conflicts and anxieties which are interfering in development can be better understood, in which communications can be recognised, made explicit, and then be taken back, to become a part of the person to whom they belong.

Background and History of the Family

June, aged four, is the third of four children. Her mother contacted the social worker in the hospital because June would not leave her mother at all. Mrs. M. told the social worker, Mrs. Goldberg, that for the last three months June had refused to stay with anyone but her mother. Mrs. M. had tried sending her to playgroup, in order to prepare her beginning school in twelve months, but she refused to stay. At home, things had become intolerable: she reported June would start to cry and scream for no particular reason, or for a petty reason—if the ketchup was on the wrong side of the plate, and then would go on sobbing unconsolably, for three hours or more. The family was feeling tyrannised, as they were all “in terror of setting her off”. In addition, June demanded to wear only a few special clothes which fitted just so—the socks must not slip down, the sleeves must be snug and not rolled over, etc. She demanded that her shoes be tightly buckled. She did not want to discard old or torn clothes. She slept well, and had a large appetite, but ate constantly, her mother reported, not out of hunger.

responseSet.title: A Latency Boy's Reaction to His Father's Death
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A Latency Boy's Reaction to His Father's Death**

William Halton

William Halton

William Halton  

This paper is about an adopted boy whose treatment was in progress when his father died suddenly. Howard was just eleven when his father, aged fifty, died from a heart attack. He had had an attack in the previous July but had made an unexpectedly good recovery. Seven years before he had two serious attacks within a year of each other, both involving several months in hospital. His father's heart condition had overshadowed Howard's life since the age of three, although the final attack occurred without warning.

When Howard came into treatment at the age of nine he was seen for a year by a woman therapist on a once a week basis. When he was transferred to me I continued on the same basis for one term but in January I increased his sessions to four times a week. Six months later, two weeks before the summer break, his father died.

The main material which I would like to discuss is drawn from the five sessions which took place within those two weeks. This material can be linked with some of the typical latency reactions to the loss of a parent described in the literature: namely the short sadness span, the inability to mourn, the avoidance of pain through the use of manic defences such as denial, triumph, contempt and control. In Howard's case, however, these defences are not used rigidly to exclude feelings of shock and grief but they are the means by which he holds himself together and protects himself from the full impact of the distress which is present underneath and which at times breaks through momentarily. But before coming to this material I would like to outline his family background and the course of his treatment up to that point.

Howard was four weeks old when he was adopted. His adoptive parents had no children of their own but three years later they also adopted a baby girl. Howard's birth was normal. For the first four weeks he was looked after by a foster-mother and after his adoption by a part-time nanny until he was four. Father was active in the mothering role and mother seems to have been in the background. Howard was bottle fed and a good feeder. He slept well and cried little. He was an active crawler and was walking by fourteen months. Toilet training began at ten months and proceeded easily. Speech development was normal. He was a placid, happy, compliant baby, except that he resisted weaning and wouldn't accept any solid food apart from Heinz baby food until he was three.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Real Life Trauma and its Implications for Therapy: Treatment of Children following the Death of a Parent**

Christopher Reeves MA

Christopher Reeves

Christopher Reeves  

Child Psychotherapist Child and Family Psychiatric Clinics, Watford and Hemel Hempstead, Herts.

“Human kind Cannot bear very much reality. Time past and time future What might have been and what has been Point to one end, which is always present”.

(T. S. Eliot: Burnt Norton 42-45.)

In one respect particularly today's conditions of work for the child psychotherapist in clinic or hospital resemble those of Freud's earliest psychoanalytic practice. As with Freud's first patients, referral is often consequent on some major traumatic experience. Parents do not habitually seek our help with the general aim of facilitating emotional growth or overcoming some intrapsychic blockage, unless this registers in fairly marked and disturbing symptoms. Their request is usually explicit—to remove some palpable complaint or redress the effects of some environmental failure. Whatever the justice of these frequent parental expectations, the incidence of such cases should perhaps prompt us to reconsider the actual effects of real trauma, and its bearing on our theory and practice. The present paper is a small contribution to such a reappraisal.

Despite the prevalence in our daily practice of such types of referral as I have just mentioned, it is arguable that the notion of “trauma” plays generally a less prominent role in psychoanalytic discourse than was the case, say, fifty years ago. Perhaps this change has resulted from a shift in the clinical interests of psychoanalysts from exclusive concern with the neuroses towards the much more extended field of the “character disorders”, depression, and psychosis, which have increasingly become the focus of technical refinements. On a theoretical level too, the growing emphasis on the earliest phases of maturation and their implications for subsequent psychic development, the rise of “object relations” theory, the stress on the importance of the mother/child bond, have all tended to demote or at least to obscure the importance originally accorded to the role of externally occasioned trauma as a pathogenic factor.

responseSet.title: Maud Mannoni: The Child, his illness, and the others. Tavistock Publications, London, 1970. Price £3.15.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Maud Mannoni: The Child, his illness, and the others. Tavistock Publications, London, 1970. Price £3.15.

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin

Margaret Rustin  

This book is an exciting and unusual one. Madame Mannoni is a French psychoanalyst trained in the tradition of Jacques Lacan. She works in a number of unorthodox ways, both in her approach to her child patient's family, and

87

because she is interested in applying the insights of psycho-analysis to cases of apparent mental retardation. She is writing here of her work with children, and its theoretical basis. A number of her analytic cases are reported on in detail, and the cases that she discusses are mainly those of severely ill children. The theoretical terminology derived from Lacan's work is unfamiliar to English readers, but a helpful glossary is provided, and reference made to an English volume on Lacan's thought. The book is translated from the French, and this work seems to have been done well.

The nub of her argument about childhood psychosis is that the sick child is struggling to attain an individual identity in the face of his own regressive urge to inhabit the personality pressed on him by parents who require of him that he serve as container for aspects of their own experience with which they cannot deal. Her assumption, therefore, is that analysis with a child is only possible if a dialogue is established between parents and analyst which offers to the parents a possibility of feeling understood as persons by their child's analyst, and thus lessening their need to use the child to express their own problems. In such a setting analysis of the child can proceed. In many of her cases, the amount of work done directly with the parents was considerable, as the child's developing integrity of personality is threatening to parents who have needed to use him in this way, since it undermines their own psychic system. Mannoni's cases are from her private practice, but it is clear from her argument that were a professional team on the English Child Guidance model available for work with these families, this would not meet, in her view, the needs of the situation. For she believes that the analyst can only comprehend the distorted and limiting identifications of her child patient if she also has access to the unconscious processes of the parents, particularly the position given to the child in the parents’ unconscious fantasy, and this she gains in her interviews with them. Sometimes she offers interpretations to parents, but she is clear that the patient in analysis is the child, while believing it essential that she convey to the parents that she understands what their difficulties are in being parents to this particular child. In periods of blockage in the child's treatment she often seems to turn to exploration of the parental attitude to the ongoing analysis for elucidation of the problem.

responseSet.title: The Complexity of Mental Pain Seen in a Six-Year-Old Child following Sudden Bereavement
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Complexity of Mental Pain Seen in a Six-Year-Old Child following Sudden Bereavement**

Martha Harris

Martha Harris

Martha Harris  

This paper is centred round a summary of seven sessions with a six-year-old boy three months after the death of his father. An attempt will be made to indicate from work done in these sessions the complicated nature of the emotions with which he was struggling in his bereavement. Some attention will be given to the confusion which could have opened up the way to a regressive illness, but also to the factors in his personality, his relationship to his external and internal objects which indicated the possibility of working through his mourning without further analytic help. I have used the word “analytic” advisedly, because the technique used in these sessions was that of following the child's communications, trying to clarify them in the transference, although with a limited number of sessions in view. Some of his material will pinpoint that aspect of mental pain which is heightened by the suffering of the surviving loved objects who share the mourning for the lost person.

Mrs. J. consulted me about her son James at the instigation of a friend of his teacher. She was a plump, small, capable-looking and attractive young woman in her early thirties, white-faced and struggling with strong emotions. In my room she began by saying,

“Ah, the sun at last. I thought it would never shine again”.

She then launched into an account of the troubles she was having with James since her husband's death three months before. She had two sons, Julian and James, aged eight and six respectively. James was more difficult in temperament; forceful, aggressive, intelligent and passionate, very attached to herself. He had not always got on so well with his father because they were too much alike. When father shouted at James, then James shouted back. Between Julian and his father there had been a more peacefully loving relationship and when her husband had died suddenly, she had expected that it would affect Julian much more adversely. On the contrary, Julian had wept and continued to weep a good deal, but it had brought him and his mother much closer together. His grief appeared to be healing; but James, instead of grieving, had become angry, unmanageable and a torment.
